slides.title: Interface Force Field
slides.lead: From atoms to evidence. A beginner’s guide to molecular mechanics and material interfaces.
slides.notes: I want to connect the atoms in a picture to a result we can check. We'll build the background first, work through rhodium, and then look at published systems where a molecular model helped explain an experiment. Every atomic drawing here is idealized. The plotted pair curves are analytic calculations from published parameters. The material results come from the cited papers and were not rerun for this talk.
slides.figure_alt: Original ideal rhodium crystal drawn as touching spheres.

slides.title: An atom has a nucleus and electrons
slides.lead: The electrons help determine how atoms interact.
claims: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons.
Electrons occupy a region around it.
A sphere is a useful drawing of size and position.
slides.notes: An atom is a unit of an element. Its positive nucleus and negative electrons give it electrical structure. The electron cloud has no hard outer wall, so a sphere is a model of atomic size. A drawing can leave out electronic detail while keeping the atomic positions we need for a material calculation. The size used in a rendering must be stated separately from a claim about electron density.
slides.figure_alt: Original single shaded sphere represents an atom’s occupied region; it is a schematic size illustration.

slides.title: Molecules connect atoms; crystals repeat a pattern
slides.lead: The arrangement depends on the material.
claims: A molecule contains atoms joined by chemical bonds.
A crystal repeats an arrangement through space.
Water and a metal surface can share one simulation box.
slides.notes: Water is a familiar molecule. A metal crystal is an extended arrangement of atoms rather than a collection of small separate molecules. At an interface, which is where two materials meet, both kinds of structure can be present. We need a model that describes each material and the interactions between them. Lines are omitted from the space-filling drawing so the occupied volume stays visible.
slides.figure_alt: Original three touching spheres represent a molecule; the accompanying text explains repeating crystals.

slides.title: Atoms push and pull on one another
slides.lead: Changing their arrangement changes the material’s energy.
claims: Atoms pushed too close resist further compression.
At suitable separations, attraction can hold a solid together.
The surrounding neighbors affect the balance.
slides.notes: Imagine compressing a metal or pulling its surface apart. Work changes how its atoms are arranged. The model assigns an energy to those arrangements and a force to each atom. The touching spheres show an ideal rhodium crystal. Their radius follows the crystal's nearest-neighbor spacing, so the rendering shows a filled solid. It is a structural illustration, with no claim that atoms are rigid billiard balls.
slides.figure_alt: Touching rhodium spheres fill the crystal volume, with readable edges and light shading.

slides.title: Can a short molecule change a metal particle’s shape?
slides.lead: A published platinum study makes the question concrete.
claims: System | Short chains of amino acids, called peptides, surround growing platinum crystals.
Change | Replacing one amino acid changes which crystal face the peptide favors.
Observation | Electron microscopy shows different particle shapes after synthesis.
Explanation | Simulations compare peptide binding on the competing faces.
slides.notes: Ruan and colleagues used peptide variants and electron microscopy to study crystal-face recognition. Their model is named CHARMM-METAL in the paper and belongs to the metal-parameter lineage incorporated into IFF. A face is a flat exposed orientation of the crystal. We'll return to the result after introducing energy, water competition and surfaces. Crystal shape is an indirect readout of selective binding, so growth conditions remain part of the evidence.

slides.title: A simulation is a controlled model experiment
slides.lead: Choose the question, construct a model, and calculate an observable.
claims: Inputs specify atoms, conditions and interactions.
The calculation produces structures, motion or energies.
A measured quantity tests the result under matched conditions.
slides.notes: An observable is a quantity we can estimate from the calculation and compare with an experiment, such as density or surface energy. A simulation can make a buried interface easier to inspect, or compare candidate molecules before synthesis. Its answer depends on the chemistry included, the mathematical approximation and the configurations explored. Agreement must be assessed for the actual question and conditions.
slides.figure_alt: Original diagram links a material question to a model, calculation, observable and experimental comparison.

slides.title: Different methods keep different physical detail
slides.lead: Choose the detail needed to answer the question.
claims: Density functional theory (DFT) describes electrons and their energy.
Classical models use effective interactions between atoms.
Learned potentials infer energies and forces from reference data.
slides.notes: Density functional theory, or DFT, is an electronic-structure method built around electron density. It can address changes in bonding and charge, with results that depend on the chosen approximation. Classical molecular mechanics replaces that electronic calculation with an energy function and parameters. Learned potentials use examples from reference calculations to approximate the energy landscape. More electronic detail usually increases cost, while a useful approximation must retain the physics the question needs.
slides.figure_alt: Original comparison of quantum, classical and learned modeling detail; scale is contextual rather than a universal benchmark.

slides.title: Compare the scale and the work actually timed
slides.lead: A single energy evaluation and a trajectory measure different work.
claims: A picosecond (ps) is one trillionth of a second. AI²BMD timing used an NVIDIA A6000 and 32 CPU cores; costs depend on the benchmark.
slides.notes: Wang and colleagues report 21 minutes for a DFT energy evaluation of 281-atom Trp-cage and 0.072 seconds for AI²BMD. Figure 2f compares energy-calculation timings; the accompanying prose calls this a simulation step. This timing benchmark does not report a trajectory duration. Kanhaiya's classical lattice protocol uses five conventional fcc cells along each axis. Four atoms per cell gives 500 atoms. It describes roughly 100 ps before stable behavior followed by 500 ps for averaging, using NPT at 298.15 K. A picosecond is one trillionth of a second. The classical paper does not provide an equivalent wall-clock timing here. Cross-paper differences in hardware, system, solvent and task prevent a universal speed ratio.

slides.title: Molecular mechanics assigns energy to atom positions
slides.lead: An energy function turns a configuration into a number.
claims: Potential energy describes the stored energy of an arrangement.
The force field contains the equation, atom types and numerical parameters.
Forces follow from how the energy changes when atoms move.
Different physical effects contribute to the total energy.
slides.notes: A configuration is a list of atomic positions, with a simulation cell when periodic boundaries are used. Molecular mechanics evaluates potential energy for that configuration. A force field supplies the functional forms and coefficients. In the common IFF-compatible form, bonded terms describe internal molecular geometry, while electrostatics and van der Waals terms describe nonbonded interactions. The complete package also needs units and rules for which atom pairs interact.

slides.title: Stretching a bond costs energy
slides.lead: Near its preferred length, a bond behaves like an effective spring.
claims: A chemical bond connects neighboring atoms.
Compression or stretching raises the spring energy.
The spring constant controls the local stiffness.
slides.notes: The spring analogy describes the shape of the energy close to equilibrium. A common harmonic form is U = (k/2)(r-r_eq)^2, with k the stiffness and r_eq the preferred bond length. Force-field families sometimes absorb the factor of one half into k, so the coefficient convention matters. A fixed harmonic bond model has a limited range and does not describe bond breaking. The drawing uses touching spheres and a separate energy diagram.
slides.figure_alt: Original touching-sphere bond-length illustration with a schematic harmonic energy curve.

slides.title: Bending an angle also costs energy
slides.lead: Three connected atoms define a bond angle.
claims: A preferred angle helps set molecular shape.
Changing that angle raises the bending energy.
Bond lengths and angles describe different motions.
slides.notes: Take two bonds that meet at the same atom. The angle between them is another coordinate of the molecule. A simple harmonic bending term rises quadratically with displacement from the preferred angle. Its stiffness affects vibrations and mechanical response. This term is distinct from an interaction between two separate molecules. The pictured arrangement is an illustrative geometry rather than a fit to a specific compound.
slides.figure_alt: Original space-filling three-atom angle diagram with separate angle-energy explanation.

slides.title: A torsion describes a twist along a bond
slides.lead: Connected groups can prefer some orientations over others.
claims: Four connected atoms define a dihedral angle.
Rotation changes the relative positions of nearby groups.
A torsion term can have several preferred orientations.
slides.notes: A dihedral angle compares the planes formed by two overlapping sets of three atoms. Rotating around the central bond can bring atoms closer together or change favorable electronic arrangements. Force fields represent the resulting energy variation with periodic terms. In a long molecule these preferences influence the shapes it can sample. Other terms, including nonbonded interactions, also contribute to the total cost of rotation.
slides.figure_alt: Original touching-sphere groups show a twist around a connected molecular axis.

slides.title: Atoms interact across a gap, too
slides.lead: Nonbonded terms describe interactions beyond a chemical bond.
claims: Van der Waals terms combine short-range repulsion and attraction.
Coulomb terms describe interactions between model charges.
Water competes with a molecule for contacts at a surface.
slides.notes: Nonbonded interactions act between atoms that are not directly joined by the relevant covalent bonds. An effective repulsive term prevents unrealistic overlap, while an attractive term can help produce cohesion. Electrostatics accounts for charges and polarity. The force field specifies exclusions and scaling for atoms connected through short bond paths, so these terms are not blindly added for every possible pair in a molecule.
slides.figure_alt: Original separated atomic groups and surface contacts illustrate nonbonded interactions.

slides.title: The Lennard-Jones curve has a wall and a well
slides.lead: This is the published rhodium 12-6 pair model.
claims: At short distance the energy rises steeply.
The attractive well lies below the separated-pair reference.
At large distance this pair energy approaches zero.
slides.notes: Lennard-Jones, abbreviated LJ, is a simple effective pair potential. The exponents identify a functional form, not a full electronic calculation. Here the original plot evaluates Kanhaiya's rhodium coefficients. The isolated pair is a teaching device. A metal crystal contains many interacting neighbors, so this curve alone does not give the total binding or elastic behavior of a solid.
slides.figure_alt: Computed rhodium Lennard-Jones 12-6 energy versus distance, with wall, minimum and asymptotic reference.

slides.title: Read the zero crossing, minimum and well depth
slides.lead: An ångström (Å) is 0.1 nm. Here, kcal/mol reports energy per mole of pairs.
claims: r₀ = 2.757 Å marks the pair minimum.
ε = 7.84 kcal/mol sets its depth.
The textbook zero-crossing σ is 2.4562 Å.
slides.notes: An angstrom, Å, is one ten-billionth of a meter. Energy is reported per mole of pairs, which scales a microscopic pair energy by Avogadro's number. Our equation is U=epsilon[(r0/r)^12-2(r0/r)^6]. Kanhaiya calls the minimum-length parameter sigma; we call it r0 to distinguish it from the zero-crossing sigma in U=4epsilon[(sigma/r)^12-(sigma/r)^6]. The curves are identical when sigma=r0/2^(1/6). At r0 the pair energy is -epsilon.
slides.figure_alt: Rhodium energy curve labels the zero crossing, pair minimum and well depth under explicitly stated conventions.

slides.title: Force is the negative slope of energy
slides.lead: The direction depends on the slope at the current distance.
claims: Positive radial force pushes atoms apart.
Negative radial force draws atoms together.
The force is zero at the pair minimum.
slides.notes: The radial force is F_r=-dU/dr. For this minimum-length 12-6 form, F_r=(12epsilon/r)[(r0/r)^12-(r0/r)^6]. The sign convention takes increasing separation as positive. Energy below zero can still have a repulsive slope. The plot is the analytic derivative of the same published pair potential, and its units are kcal per mole per angstrom. It is not a measured force trace.
slides.figure_alt: Original analytic radial-force curve; positive force is repulsive, negative force attractive, and zero occurs at r0.

slides.title: Work the rhodium numbers
slides.lead: Substitute a distance into the energy and force equations.
claims: An energy below zero can still produce repulsion. The slope sets the force.
slides.notes: These rounded values come from direct analytic evaluation of the published 12-6 rhodium parameters. At 2.500 Å, the energy is negative while the force is positive because the separation is shorter than the minimum. At 2.757 Å the energy is -7.84 and the force vanishes. At 3.000 Å the force is attractive. The table's force unit is kcal/(mol Å), and energy is kcal/mol of pairs. Extra digits in the check file document arithmetic, not higher physical precision.

slides.title: Changing the metal changes the pair curve
slides.lead: Rhodium, iridium, calcium and strontium use one published parameter table.
claims: Rh and Ir have deeper, shorter wells in this set.
Ca and Sr have wider, shallower wells.
Each curve uses its own minimum length and well depth.
slides.notes: Kanhaiya Table 1 gives Rh r0=2.757 Å and epsilon=7.84 kcal/mol; Ir 2.785 and 9.20; alpha-Ca 4.025 and 3.36; alpha-Sr 4.379 and 3.40. These are elemental fcc model parameters. They do not establish that a material remains chemically stable in every environment. For example, reactivity in water needs an appropriate model. The original plots compare the specified pair functions at their published values.
slides.figure_alt: Original energy and force comparisons for Rh, Ir, alpha-Ca and alpha-Sr using one primary table.

slides.title: A solid adds interactions with many neighbors
slides.lead: A pair well depth and a surface energy have different units.
claims: Pair energy | ε describes one pair’s well depth in energy per mole of pairs.
Bulk cohesion | The model adds interactions across an extended atomic arrangement.
Surface work | Creating a surface changes contacts across an area.
Connection | With fixed geometry and length parameters, the LJ energy sum scales with ε.
slides.notes: The pair sum runs over each distinct unordered atom pair. A solid's equilibrium spacing balances interactions with multiple neighbor shells. Cleaving a solid changes many terms and allows atoms to relax. Surface energy is reported in joules per square meter, whereas epsilon has energy units. Fitting a surface target therefore requires an actual surface calculation, a normalization and stated conditions. There is no universal unit conversion from epsilon to gamma.

slides.title: A mixed pair needs an explicit combining rule
slides.lead: This Rh–Ca example uses the CVFF geometric rule.
claims: r₀,ij = √(r₀,ii r₀,jj) = 3.3312 Å.
εij = √(εii εjj) = 5.1325 kcal/mol.
At 4.000 Å, the mixed-pair energy is −2.8533 kcal/mol.
slides.notes: A combining rule generates a cross interaction from the two like-atom parameters. This example uses geometric means for both minimum lengths and well depths, following the selected CVFF family convention. Other families use different length rules. The arithmetic is an illustration of how a rule is consumed. It supplies no evidence that a Rh-Ca alloy is accurately represented. Alloy charge, phase stability and electronic effects need their own evidence.
slides.figure_alt: Original Rh-Ca mixed-pair curve from declared geometric combining rules; it is a mathematical example.

slides.title: Charges add electrical attraction or repulsion
slides.lead: Opposite model charges attract; equal signs repel.
claims: Coulomb energy is proportional to q_i q_j/r.
For +1e and −1e at 3 Å in vacuum, U = −110.688 kcal/mol.
Water, polarization and the ion model change the physical problem.
slides.notes: The symbol e is the magnitude of the elementary charge. Using k=332.064 kcal Å/(mol e²), the point-charge calculation is U=k(+1)(-1)/3. These are illustrative charges in vacuum and are not the charges on rhodium atoms. Real ions also have size and other interactions. In water, solvent orientation, screening and polarization affect the result, so the vacuum value cannot be used as an ion-pair energy in solution.
slides.figure_alt: Original Coulomb energy example for opposite unit charges in vacuum, with explicit omitted solvent effects.

slides.title: A small cluster counts each pair once
slides.lead: Three touching Rh atoms provide a transparent energy sum.
claims: The equilateral triangle has three distinct pairs.
Each separation is r₀ = 2.757 Å; each pair contributes −7.84 kcal/mol.
The total is −23.52 kcal/mol of clusters.
slides.notes: The pairs are atom 1 with 2, atom 1 with 3, and atom 2 with 3. Summing each once gives three times -7.84. The sphere diameter equals the isolated-pair minimum in this deliberately simple illustration. This is not a fragment cut from the equilibrium fcc crystal. No relaxation, long-time stability or preference over other cluster shapes has been calculated. A larger system uses the same counting idea while boundary and cutoff rules also matter.
slides.figure_alt: Original equilateral three-atom Rh pair-minimum illustration and three-pair energy sum.

slides.title: Molecular mechanics makes repeated sampling practical
slides.lead: Simple interactions let us evaluate many configurations.
claims: Motion | Follow atoms through many short time steps.
Interfaces | Include a surface, solvent and molecules in the same box.
Statistics | Estimate averages and fluctuations from sampled configurations.
Scope | Use a model tested for the chemistry and observables of interest.
slides.notes: A single low-energy structure may miss the many arrangements present at a finite temperature. The lower cost of classical interactions makes repeated energy and force evaluation practical. This helps sample molecular conformations, water exchange and surface binding. The benefit depends on the model and workload. A fast trajectory can still sample too little time or use the wrong surface chemistry.

slides.title: Parameters connect equations to physical measurements
slides.lead: Each parameter has a physical role, with coupled effects.
claims: Size and packing | Length parameters influence density and lattice spacing.
Cohesion | Energy parameters influence surface work and adhesion.
Polarity | Model charges influence electric interactions and adsorption.
Internal stiffness | Bond and angle terms influence geometry and vibrations.
slides.notes: Parameterization chooses coefficients so the model reflects the material of interest. Structural data constrain packing and bonding geometry. Surface and immersion measurements constrain interactions across material boundaries. Dipole moments and other electrical data help constrain charge assignments. These effects are coupled. Several parameters may affect the same observable, and a fitted coefficient is not necessarily a uniquely measured atom property.

slides.title: Fitting and testing answer different questions
slides.lead: Reserve evidence that the fitting process cannot use.
claims: Fit | Choose parameters against declared calibration targets.
Test | Evaluate another relevant observable after the choice is fixed.
If a test guides revision | Treat it as development evidence and find a fresh test.
Report | Keep reference uncertainty and model disagreement visible.
slides.notes: For the rhodium example, density or lattice size and surface energy are calibration targets. The elastic properties are predictions beyond those targets. This separation lets us ask whether a useful surface model also reproduces mechanical response. A reserved test loses independence if its outcome is used to tune a parameter, choose a model family or adjust a fitting weight. The published paper is not described here as a prospectively blinded campaign.

slides.title: A parameter should have a defensible physical role
slides.lead: Interpretability helps explain a result and recognize a failure.
claims: Ask which measurements constrain the parameter.
Check whether its size and sign make chemical sense.
Change it deliberately and inspect affected observables.
Recognize when the chosen equation cannot reproduce the behavior.
slides.notes: Physically interpretable means we can explain why a parameter is present and how it relates to the modeled chemistry. For example, a length parameter changes the distance scale while an energy parameter changes cohesion. Interpretation does not make the fit unique or guarantee transfer to a new compound. The rhodium mechanical limit will show why a sensible parameter set can still be restricted by its functional form.

slides.title: IFF connects inorganic surfaces with molecules
slides.lead: The Interface Force Field is a compatible parameter framework.
claims: Inorganic part | Parameters and surface models for supported materials.
Molecular part | Compatible descriptions of water, polymers and biomolecules.
Interface | Cross interactions follow the chosen family’s equations and rules.
Evidence | Structural and energetic comparisons support a stated scope.
slides.notes: IFF stands for Interface Force Field. The 2013 paper establishes a framework for combining inorganic and molecular components while retaining chemically interpretable parameters and thermodynamic comparisons. Its purpose includes the boundary where a biomolecule or polymer meets a solid. Coverage is compound-specific. A supported force-field family still needs suitable parameters, charge assignments and surface models for the proposed system.

slides.title: Compatibility is an equation-level requirement
slides.lead: A familiar force-field name alone does not define the model.
claims: Potential and units | Match the functional form and numerical units.
Length convention | Distinguish a pair minimum from a zero crossing.
Cross interactions | Preserve mixing rules, exclusions and scaling.
Readback | Check energies and forces from the files the engine consumes.
slides.notes: IFF has been integrated with common molecular force-field families, including CHARMM, AMBER, CVFF, OPLS and PCFF in the supported contexts described by the papers. These families do not share every convention. A valid export must preserve the intended interactions, including the treatment of short bond paths and unlike atom types. Reading exported coefficients is useful, but a numerical energy and force comparison checks the consumed interpretation.

slides.title: A silica surface changes its chemistry in water
slides.lead: pH and surface preparation affect which groups a molecule sees.
claims: Surface groups | Silica can present neutral silanol groups and charged siloxide groups.
Solution | pH affects protonation; ions balance electrical charge.
Molecule | Positive peptide groups can pair with negative surface sites.
Model | Choose surface chemistry to match the experimental sample.
slides.notes: A silanol is a silicon-oxygen-hydrogen group at the surface. Losing its proton leaves a negatively charged siloxide group. The particle size, solution and preparation influence the extent of this change. The silica papers show why a surface labeled only SiO2 is incomplete. We use their published chemical and adsorption evidence here. The later correction to the 2014 paper changes density-profile plots, which this deck does not reproduce.

slides.title: Rhodium begins with a repeating fcc cell
slides.lead: Face-centered cubic, or fcc, names the crystal arrangement.
claims: Atoms occupy the corners and face centers of a cube.
Shared boundary atoms give four atoms per conventional cell.
The reference cube has a = 3.8032 Å.
slides.notes: A unit cell is a building block that can reproduce the crystal by translation. A conventional fcc cell contains four independent atomic sites after sharing corner and face sites with neighboring cells. The corrected source cell has cubic edge 3.8032 Å. Boundary spheres in a drawing can show copies of shared atoms, so their visible count is not the count of independent atoms. Crystal-contact spheres have radius a/(2sqrt(2)), consistent with touching nearest neighbors.
slides.figure_alt: Original conventional face-centered cubic Rh cell with touching spheres on corners and face centers.

slides.title: Repeat the cell to build a supercell
slides.lead: The boundary conditions define what lies beyond the box.
claims: A 5 × 5 × 5 array contains 500 atoms.
Periodic boundaries repeat the box in space.
Box size and periodic images can affect the result.
slides.notes: Five cells in each of three directions gives 125 conventional cells. Multiplying by four atoms per fcc cell gives 500 atoms, the lattice-protocol size described in the paper's SI. A smaller drawing may be used to show the pattern clearly. Periodic boundaries mimic extended material through copies; surfaces and isolated molecules require appropriate extra space and boundary treatment. Convergence checks assess whether a larger box changes the observable.
slides.figure_alt: Original touching-sphere supercell illustration; displayed geometry illustrates periodic repetition.

slides.title: Expose a surface by cleaving the solid
slides.lead: The orientation determines which atomic layer is exposed.
claims: The label (111) identifies one crystallographic orientation.
Separating a solid removes contacts across the cut.
The surface atoms can relax after exposure.
slides.notes: Miller indices such as (111) label an orientation in a crystal. The cut shown here creates equivalent parallel faces. Atoms at those faces have fewer neighbors across the missing solid, and their positions can adjust. The pictured slab is idealized and constructed for explanation. It is not a reconstruction of an experimental surface or a newly simulated rhodium trajectory.
slides.figure_alt: Original Rh(111) slab schematic uses touching spheres to show two exposed surfaces.

slides.title: Two new faces require a factor of two
slides.lead: Surface energy divides the cleavage work by the new area.
claims: γ ≈ (〈Ecleaved〉 − 〈Eunified〉) / (2A).
A is the area of one face; cleaving makes two equivalent faces.
Use matched atom counts and consistent simulation conditions.
The energy-difference estimate needs a justified entropy approximation.
slides.notes: The angle brackets denote an average over sampled configurations. If two equivalent faces of area A are created, the total newly exposed area is 2A. Kanhaiya's metal method compares matched unified and cleaved boxes. The full free-energy expression includes entropy; the SI estimates a small correction for the metal conditions studied. This approximation needs to be reassessed for a different interface, temperature or molecular adsorption process.

slides.title: Excellent agreement can be a calibration result
slides.lead: These Rh measurements helped choose the metal parameters.
claims: The surface reference can include polycrystalline samples. The paper explains its use as a (111) estimate.
slides.notes: Kanhaiya Table 2 reports a five-cell length, 5a, rather than a single cell edge. The published 12-6 model gives the same rounded value as the reference. Table 3 reports Rh(111) surface energy 2.643 J/m² for both LJ families versus reference 2.64±0.02. These comparisons test reproduction of calibration data. The SI discusses experimental face mixtures and the approximation between surface free energy and the energy-difference method. Published values are reproduced here as facts and were not rerun.

slides.title: Minimization finds a nearby low-energy arrangement
slides.lead: Move atoms downhill until the chosen stopping rule is met.
claims: Relax an initially strained geometry.
The result depends on the starting configuration.
A local minimum can coexist with lower minima elsewhere.
slides.notes: Energy minimization uses forces or gradients to reduce the potential energy. It is useful for removing unrealistic close contacts and relaxing a structure before dynamics. It does not assign a physical time to the movement down the landscape. A minimizer can stop in a local basin, so several starting configurations or broader sampling may be needed. The landscape is an original explanatory sketch.
slides.figure_alt: Original schematic energy landscape distinguishes a nearby local minimum from other basins.

slides.title: Molecular dynamics advances motion in short steps
slides.lead: Use forces and atomic masses to update positions and velocities.
claims: Calculate forces from the current configuration.
Advance a short time step, then calculate again.
The metal study uses a 1 fs time step, one quadrillionth of a second.
slides.notes: Newton's equation connects acceleration to force through atomic mass. A molecular-dynamics integrator repeatedly updates positions and velocities using that relationship. A femtosecond, fs, is one quadrillionth of a second. Temperature and pressure controls set the intended statistical conditions, and their settings affect sampling. A successful short run does not prove convergence. Any motion in our diagrams is illustrative and does not represent a new material trajectory.
slides.figure_alt: Original loop diagram connects positions, forces, velocities and the next time step.

slides.title: A trajectory becomes evidence through an observable
slides.lead: Specify what is averaged and how uncertainty is assessed.
claims: Density | Average the mass per sampled volume.
Surface energy | Compare matched energy averages and area.
Diffusion | Relate particle displacement to elapsed time.
Uncertainty | Check fluctuations, sampling duration and box size.
slides.notes: A trajectory is a time-ordered series of atomic configurations. Turning it into a material result requires an estimator with a reference state and conditions. Neighboring time samples are correlated, so a large frame count does not automatically mean many independent observations. Block averages, repeated runs and convergence checks help assess sampling. Experimental uncertainty and model error are separate sources of disagreement.

slides.title: Rhodium mechanics exposes the pair model’s limit
slides.lead: Surface agreement does not establish mechanical accuracy.
claims: The central-force pair framework constrains C₁₂/C₄₄ = 1. Rh has larger errors in stretching and shear.
slides.notes: Moduli describe stiffness under different deformations. K is the bulk modulus for volume compression, E is Young's modulus for uniaxial stretching, and G is the shear modulus. This table uses the selected experimental reference d in Kanhaiya Table 5; other reference values are listed in the paper. The 12-6 bulk modulus is about 6.5% lower than 276 GPa, but its Young's and shear moduli differ much more. The Cauchy-type central-force restriction limits independent elastic behavior. The examples are published predictions beyond the lattice and surface calibration, not newly rerun measurements.

slides.title: An alloy needs evidence beyond a mixing rule
slides.lead: AlNi illustrates why chemical assignment matters.
claims: Composition | An alloy combines different elements in one material.
Charge model | The published AlNi model uses Al +0.39e and Ni −0.39e.
Constraint | The full structure must preserve overall electrical neutrality.
Evidence | Charge assignment uses alloy formation energetics and chemical reasoning.
slides.notes: Liu's SI states that alloy charges were obtained using pure-metal pair potentials and experimental formation energies, with extended-Born reasoning to interpret chemical trends. The AlNi base assignment is +0.39e for Al and -0.39e for Ni. These are model partial charges. They are not a unique experimental partition of electrons. A neutral elemental metal model cannot simply be copied into every alloy without examining polarity, phase and structure.

slides.title: Defects and polarization change the model question
slides.lead: A missing atom or a mobile electron cloud can require new terms.
claims: Defect | Removing an atom changes its neighbors and the charge assignment.
AlNi evidence | Different charge-redistribution hypotheses change raw defect energies.
Polarization | A metal’s electron cloud responds to nearby charges.
Model choice | Compare a suitable pair model, many-body model or polarizable extension.
slides.notes: A defect is a departure from the ideal crystal, such as a missing atom. L18SI Table S2 varies how charge left by an AlNi vacancy is assigned among nearby atoms. Its raw molecular-mechanics energies depend on that hypothesis and are not measured formation free energies. A fixed neutral LJ model also lacks an explicit responding electron cloud. Geada's gold extension adds a charged core-shell response. Many-body models such as EAM can address other metal-specific behavior, with their own scope and interface limitations.

slides.title: Real systems test different parts of a model
slides.lead: Each example names an experiment and a limit.
claims: Platinum | Crystal-face preference and particle shape.
Silica | Peptide adsorption and water wetting.
Bone mineral | pH-dependent surfaces and hydration.
Cement and gold | Grain attraction and metal polarization.
slides.notes: We have enough background to return to real questions. These six published examples use related interface modeling ideas across different chemistry. Some establish a mechanism through matched trends, while others compare a numerical surface property. Their evidential strength differs. A success on one interface does not validate all supported compounds or every property of the same material.

slides.title: Peptide chemistry steers platinum crystal shape
slides.lead: Can changing one amino acid alter which faces survive growth?
claims: System | Peptides coat platinum nanocrystals growing in solution.
Model result | A phenyl ring creates binding contrast between (111) and (100) faces.
Experiment | Replacing L with F in TLT produced TFT and shifted cubes toward tetrahedra.
Limit | Shape is an indirect binding readout under the tested synthesis conditions.
slides.notes: Ruan et al., Nano Letters 2013, pp. 842-844, Figures 2-3. The CHARMM-METAL model, an IFF metal-model predecessor, describes competition between water and peptides. Phenylalanine's ring can lie on (111) but has an unfavorable geometry on (100), reducing adsorption there. Strong binding to (111) alone did not correlate with tetrahedral yield; contrast between faces mattered. The TLT-to-TFT substitution and microscopy provided an experimental test of the proposed recognition principle. The calculations did not simulate the complete synthesis reaction.

slides.title: A silica-binding peptide must fit the surface
slides.lead: Why can two changes to the same peptide have opposite effects?
claims: System | Short peptides bind to silica nanoparticles in water.
Model result | Charge pairing, hydrogen bonds and molecular flexibility control contacts.
Experiment | Two histidine-to-alanine mutations gave opposite adsorption trends.
Limit | The modeled surface chemistry must represent the measured particles.
slides.notes: Patwardhan et al., JACS 2012, Figure 10 and Table 3, pp. 6251-6253. Replacing histidine at one position relieved conformational strain and allowed better contacts. Replacing a terminal histidine removed useful contacts and weakened binding. Adsorption assays and zeta-potential data supported the computed relative trends. A hydrogen bond is an attractive interaction involving a hydrogen-bearing group and a suitable electronegative site. Zeta potential measures an electrical property of the particle's moving liquid boundary, rather than a direct image of individual charges.

slides.title: Surface groups change how water wets silica
slides.lead: Can a model reproduce the heat released when dry silica meets water?
claims: System | Silica surfaces with different exposed oxygen and hydroxyl groups.
Model result | Water affinity changes with the surface groups.
Experiment | Immersion heat was 160 ± 5 mJ/m²; the TIP3P simulation gave 160 ± 2.
Limit | Hydration energy helped choose the parameters, so this is a calibration comparison.
slides.notes: Emami et al., Chemistry of Materials 2014, section 4.1 and Figure 5, pp. 2653-2654. Heat of immersion is the energy released when a dry surface enters water; values here are its positive magnitude. The SPC, TIP3P and PCFF water models gave 167, 160 and 157 mJ/m² respectively, so the selected comparison explicitly names TIP3P. Section 4.2 and Figure 6 also compare wetting as surface chemistry changes. The 2016 correction revises density-profile Figures 8-9; it leaves the immersion and contact-angle data used here unchanged. These comparisons support a specified surface/water model and are not a universal held-out accuracy score. The paper states that hydration energies of Q3 surfaces were among the quantities used to refine nonbonded parameters, so this numerical agreement is a calibration check.

slides.title: Bone mineral presents a pH-dependent surface
slides.lead: Which surface does water or a biomolecule actually encounter?
claims: System | Hydroxyapatite, a major mineral in bone and teeth.
Model result | Protonation changes surface composition, hydration and facet stability.
Experiment | Facet-averaged immersion energies were compared with calorimetry.
Limit | Surface preparation and hydration depth complicate a one-to-one comparison.
slides.notes: Lin and Heinz, JPCC 2016, Table 7 and discussion, pp. 4986-4987. Hydroxyapatite contains calcium, phosphate and hydroxide. Changing pH changes surface protonation and calcium content in the constructed models. The work compares immersion energies and hydration-stabilized crystal shapes with experimental data. Dry-sample calorimetry reports values around 600-700 mJ/m², while broader literature values depend on preparation. The paper explains how facet weighting and hydration history affect comparisons. This evidence concerns mineral surfaces; it establishes no drug efficacy or clinical prediction.

slides.title: Grinding aids reduce attraction between cement grains
slides.lead: Why can a little organic additive help freshly broken grains stay apart?
claims: System | Tricalcium silicate surfaces with organic amines and alcohols.
Model result | Adsorbed molecules separate surfaces and weaken electrical attraction.
Experiment | Predicted trends correlate with measured grinding-aid efficiency.
Limit | Ideal face-to-face attraction is one part of a working cement mill.
slides.notes: Mishra, Flatt and Heinz, JPCC 2013, Figure 6 and section 6, pp. 10426-10427. The model compares reconstructed dry, hydroxylated and organically covered surfaces. MDIPA and TIPA show greater reductions in attraction than the weaker aids, in the same qualitative order as grinding observations. The comparison is a trend across additives, rather than a direct measurement of each atomistic agglomeration energy. Direct C3S cleavage data are limited and some calibration checks use related phases. Fracture, roughness, coverage and processing conditions also influence milling performance.

slides.title: Gold’s electrons respond to nearby charges
slides.lead: When does a fixed metal pair model miss an electrical response?
claims: System | Gold in contact with water, ions and charged peptides.
Model result | A polarizable extension responds to nearby charges and alters ion binding.
Experiment | Water-monolayer adsorption was −13.0 ± 0.1 kcal/mol on modeled Au(111); references were −13 and −15.5.
Limit | The experimental references are polycrystalline; ion profiles are model predictions.
slides.notes: Geada et al., Nature Communications 2018, Table 2 p. 6 and Figure 5 p. 7. A harmonically coupled charged core-shell pair on each metal atom models polarization. The water-monolayer comparison above is for the polarizable (111) model, with experimental reference differences and surface mismatch retained. The nonpolarizable model already gives similar liquid-water energetics; induced charges matter differently for ion contact. The interfacial-tension experimental entry is an upper bound, so it must not be treated as an exact measurement. The extension does not give a general model of chemical reactions or arbitrary electrode conditions.

slides.title: Choose the observable before judging the result
slides.lead: The experimental question determines the strength of the claim.
claims: Shape | Morphology can support a binding mechanism while growth also matters.
Adsorption | Match molecule, surface state and solution.
Surface energy | Keep reference state, area and entropy assumptions explicit.
Prediction | State whether the comparison was used to fit the parameters.
slides.notes: Across the examples, the strongest conclusion follows the actual measured quantity. A morphology trend, an adsorption assay and a calorimetric energy are different tests. Keep conditions attached to the result. A model that explains one trend may still have important numerical errors elsewhere, as the rhodium mechanical table shows. New chemistry or an altered surface calls for renewed evidence.

slides.title: The IFF Agent carries evidence through eight steps
slides.lead: The workflow connects the material question to a reviewed result.
claims: Scientific choices remain linked to references.
The model and its exported interpretation stay inspectable.
Review can qualify, restrict or withhold a result.
slides.notes: The approved public workflow has eight steps: Intake, References, Model, Contract, Run and fit, Validate, Export readback, and Review and disposition. The workflow aims to carry decisions and evidence through a calculation without losing their context. Implementing this workflow does not establish that any new material package has passed fitting, independent validation or scientific adoption.
slides.figure_alt: Original eight-step IFF Agent workflow with the approved public step names.

slides.title: Define the question before running the fit
slides.lead: The first four steps establish what the result must mean.
claims: 1. Intake | Specify material, phase, conditions and intended observable.
2. References | Select primary evidence and keep its uncertainty.
3. Model | Assign chemical types, charges and a force-field family.
4. Contract | Declare calibration targets, reserved tests and acceptance limits.
slides.notes: A fit/test contract is a plan for assessing a bounded model, including which measurements may tune it and which are reserved. The model assignment must include the chosen family conventions. Changing the chemistry, references or intended use can change which model and tests are appropriate. Keeping these choices inspectable lets a reviewer reconstruct why a coefficient set was considered suitable.

slides.title: Run, test, read back, then review
slides.lead: The remaining four steps preserve the meaning of the result.
claims: 5. Run and fit | Calculate with source-grounded structures and declared settings.
6. Validate | Check reserved observables and convergence.
7. Export readback | Compare the actual files consumed by each engine.
8. Review and disposition | Record a qualified result and its supported scope.
slides.notes: An export can be syntactically valid while changing units, mixing or length conventions. Readback compares the consumed model against the intended one, including energy and forces where relevant. Validation also needs numerical convergence and suitable scientific comparisons. A final review can accept a bounded use, narrow it or withhold a material claim. Execution receipts prove that operations happened; scientific evidence determines what their results establish.

slides.title: A repeatable answer can still be inaccurate
slides.lead: Repeatability checks execution; accuracy needs an external reference.
claims: Repeatability | Reuse the same inputs and obtain consistent outputs.
Accuracy | Compare the relevant observable against suitable evidence.
Model error | A stable, converged calculation can disagree with experiment.
Example | The Rh pair model repeats its limited mechanical response.
slides.notes: If every input, coefficient and numerical setting is preserved, rerunning a calculation should produce consistent behavior within its statistical and numerical variability. That is useful evidence about execution. A physical model can reproduce the same wrong answer. Rhodium's elastic mismatch illustrates this distinction even when its density and surface targets are reproduced well.

slides.title: Use DFT when electron rearrangement matters
slides.lead: Electronic structure can be the central unknown.
claims: Investigate bonding changes, charge transfer or local electronic states.
Choose and test the density-functional approximation.
Check system size, sampling and reference dependence.
Use suitable experiments or higher-level calculations for comparison.
slides.notes: DFT evaluates electronic energy using an electron-density framework. It is useful when a fixed-chemistry model cannot represent the event being studied, such as a chemical reaction or changing electronic distribution. Results depend on the functional, electronic setup and sampled structures. DFT is an approximation with property-specific errors. A more detailed method still needs evidence for the target observable.

slides.title: Use classical IFF for supported interface sampling
slides.lead: A validated effective model can describe many configurations.
claims: Represent the material’s chemistry and surface state.
Use compatible molecular and inorganic parameters.
Sample long enough for the intended observable.
Test transfer to a changed composition or environment.
slides.notes: Classical IFF is useful when its effective interactions and surface models are appropriate and the need is to explore molecular configurations or interface behavior. Fixed-topology bonded models do not automatically form and break bonds. A fixed neutral metal model also lacks explicit changing charge. The published example papers support defined uses. They do not grant blanket transfer to untested compounds, defects or reaction pathways.

slides.title: Use a learned potential within its supported data domain
slides.lead: A model’s training coverage shapes the questions it can answer.
claims: Train against suitable reference energies and forces.
Include relevant structures, compositions and conditions.
Test on evidence that did not guide development.
Examine uncertainty when entering a new environment.
slides.notes: A learned potential estimates an energy function from data. MACE is one primary example of this approach; AI²BMD applies a learned quantum-based strategy to biomolecular simulation. Architecture alone does not determine transfer. A model trained around one set of structures can make unreliable predictions when bonding, composition or configuration changes beyond its coverage. Its reference method also contributes uncertainty.

slides.title: Compare methods against the same physical question
slides.lead: The useful choice depends on detail, sampling and evidence.
slides.notes: This comparison describes tendencies rather than a universal ranking. A fair performance claim specifies the same observable, system, target error and workload, with hardware and sampling costs. Hybrid approaches can combine methods when needed. Learned and classical models both require suitable validation; quantum calculations also need convergence and a defensible reference approximation. The method name alone cannot settle accuracy.

slides.title: What these figures establish
slides.lead: Each visual has a specific evidential role.
claims: Structures | Idealized space-filling models explain geometry.
Pair plots | Analytic evaluations use published parameters and stated equations.
Motion | Illustrative movement explains an operation or force direction.
Material comparisons | Published results are cited and were not rerun here.
slides.notes: The new curves can be rebuilt from the public source scripts and parameter table. Reproducing their arithmetic establishes correct evaluation of the equation. It does not independently validate the equation as a model of rhodium. The surface, mechanics and application examples refer to published studies. No new fit, material trajectory, experiment or adopted parameter package is presented in this deck.

slides.title: Ask what would change your confidence
slides.lead: A useful review can name both supporting evidence and failure conditions.
claims: Chemistry | Does the structure match the phase, surface and solution?
Reference | Is the observable and its uncertainty suitable?
Sampling | Do time, size and numerical choices leave the result stable?
Scope | Which new observation would require a different model?
slides.notes: For a peptide, check which face and solution were used. For bone mineral, check the protonation and hydration history. For a force-field export, check the consumed equation and units. For rhodium mechanics, keep the deformation mode visible. These checks make the claim reviewable and help decide when a more detailed or different model is required.

slides.title: IFF makes an interface a testable atomic model
slides.lead: Its value comes from chemistry, compatibility and evidence together.
claims: Connect a solid with water, polymers or biomolecules.
Give the parameters a physical interpretation.
Check structural and energetic properties against stated measurements.
Carry the result with conditions, uncertainty and limits.
slides.notes: The Interface Force Field provides a framework for supported inorganic and molecular interactions in one compatible description. Its papers show how chemical assignment, surface models and property comparisons can make interface simulations useful. The examples span several types of evidence. The size of a claimed success should remain tied to the actual tested system and observable.

slides.title: Some questions require a different model
slides.lead: Change the method when the missing physics controls the answer.
claims: Reactions | Bond formation and breaking require suitable reactive or electronic treatment.
Changing charges | Polarization and charge transfer need appropriate terms.
New defects or phases | Reassess chemical assignments and evidence.
Unsupported interfaces | Obtain relevant parameters and independent tests.
slides.notes: An ordinary fixed-topology IFF model has a stated set of atoms, terms and charges. Reactive extensions and polarizable models expand particular capabilities, with separate parameterization and validation. The gold extension is one such bounded example. A model should be selected by the physical question and tested within the proposed conditions. An unfamiliar system can fall outside several available models at once.

slides.title: Read the primary evidence
slides.lead: The full bibliography and source notes travel with the deck.
claims: Foundation | Heinz et al. 2013, IFF framework.
Worked metal | Kanhaiya et al. 2021, paper and supplementary methods.
Applications | Ruan 2013; Patwardhan 2012; Emami 2014; Lin 2016; Mishra 2013; Geada 2018.
Methods | Hohenberg and Kohn 1964; Batatia et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2024.
slides.notes: The citation manifest lists source titles, DOI links, precise use and reuse status. Presenter notes keep the context of each comparison. Original plots and drawings avoid redistributing paper figures. The source rebuild instructions identify how the deck and analytic curves were made. The appendix defines equation conventions and retains the rhodium evidence table and experimental qualifications.

slides.title: Questions
slides.lead: Which observation would make us change the model?
claims: What is the physical question?
Which measurement would test the answer?
Which missing effect could change the conclusion?
slides.notes: I would start with the observable we need to trust. The method, parameter choices and checks follow from that question. A useful next experiment or calculation distinguishes plausible explanations and can change the decision. The appendix is available for equations, conventions and the numerical evidence behind the worked examples.

slides.title: Equations and units
slides.lead: Use one declared convention throughout a calculation.
claims: Utotal = Ubonds + Uangles + Utorsions + UCoulomb + UvdW.
U12-6 = ε[(r₀/r)¹² − 2(r₀/r)⁶].
Fᵣ = (12ε/r)[(r₀/r)¹² − (r₀/r)⁶].
UCoulomb = kq_i q_j/r. Energy is kcal/mol; length is Å; force is kcal/(mol Å).
slides.notes: Bond, angle and torsion functions depend on the chosen family, as do exclusions and scale factors for short bond paths. The written radial force is positive for increasing separation. The constants and coefficient meanings must be consistent with the unit system. The analytic plots sum explicitly defined pair interactions and do not replace a complete periodic simulation with its cutoff and electrostatic choices.

slides.title: The paper’s sigma is a minimum-length parameter
slides.lead: Read the equation before transferring a coefficient.
claims: Paper form uses σpaper = r₀ in ε[(r₀/r)¹² − 2(r₀/r)⁶].
Textbook and lj/cut form uses 4ε[(σzero/r)¹² − (σzero/r)⁶].
The conversion is σzero = r₀ / 2^(1/6).
slides.notes: The symbol sigma alone is ambiguous across sources. Kanhaiya Equation 1 uses it at the energy minimum, while the common lj/cut form uses it at the zero crossing. Epsilon remains the well depth for this algebraic conversion. Entering 2.757 Å as the zero-crossing sigma would define a different pair potential. Preserve the equation with the number and verify the consumed energy curve.

slides.title: The 9-6 and 12-6 wells are different functions
slides.lead: Each form has its own fitted coefficients and mixing rules.
claims: 12-6 | U = ε[(r₀/r)¹² − 2(r₀/r)⁶]. Rh uses r₀ = 2.757 Å and ε = 7.84 kcal/mol.
9-6 | U = ε[2(r₀/r)⁹ − 3(r₀/r)⁶]. Rh uses r₀ = 2.807 Å and ε = 6.38 kcal/mol.
At the minimum | Both written forms give U(r₀) = −ε and zero radial force.
Transfer | Changing the radius alone cannot convert one function into the other.
slides.notes: The different repulsive exponents change the shape and curvature of the well. Their fitted coefficients are not interchangeable. The 12-6 conversion between zero crossing and minimum length is an exact rewriting of one function. Moving from a 12-6 function to a 9-6 function changes the model. Kanhaiya reports separate rhodium coefficients for both forms in Table 1. Host-family combination rules must also be retained.

slides.title: Parameters and worked-number checks
slides.lead: Published coefficients feed independently checked analytic calculations.
claims: Derived checks include mixed Rh–Ca ε = 5.1325, vacuum charge energy −110.688, and triangle energy −23.52 kcal/mol.
slides.notes: All four elemental-metal rows come from Kanhaiya Table 1 and are the 12-6 family. The zero-crossing sigma is derived from the minimum-length r0. The public science-checks file contains unrounded values and algebraic assertions at the minimum and for the derivative. The Coulomb and cluster examples use the deliberately restricted geometries stated on their slides. These computations verify arithmetic and convention handling, rather than new material accuracy.

slides.title: Rhodium evidence and uncertainty
slides.lead: Calibration, prediction and reference uncertainty remain separate.
claims: Other K references are 270, 271 and 269 GPa. The selected reference here is 276 GPa.
The paper reports C₁₂/C₄₄ = 1 for its central-force pair framework.
slides.notes: Kanhaiya Tables 2, 3 and 5 provide these values. The lattice and surface rows were calibration targets. The elastic rows are predictions beyond those targets. Selected E and G references are listed in the main mechanical slide; Poisson ratio appears in this appendix, and other reference values remain in the paper. The Rh-water table gives an experimental upper bound, so it is excluded as a direct accuracy benchmark. L18SI's AlNi vacancy comparisons separately report raw MM energies of 5.49, 4.57 and 2.59 eV for first/second-shell charge partitions 100/0, 67/33 and 0/100. Those hypotheses are not measured formation free energies.

slides.lead: All diagrams and plots are original; papers support the scientific facts.
claims: IFF | Heinz et al. Langmuir 2013. DOI 10.1021/la3038846.
Applications | Ruan, Patwardhan, Emami, Lin, Mishra and Geada papers are listed in the citation manifest.
Rebuild | Source equations, parameters, notes and licenses accompany the deck.
